author: reek
body: know-a is what player 0 has legitimately learned about player 1's hand; know-b is what player 1 has learned about player 0's. lib-a and lib-b are each player's knowledge of their OWN library order (from a scry, brainstorm, etc.). All start empty. know-for / lib-for read the acting player's own belief; a draw consumes the top of that player's library knowledge.

author: reek
body: Belief-model integration. Before its normal casts, the acting player casts a reveal (Duress) if it holds one; casting it records the opponent's remaining hand into the acting player's Knowledge -- the one point where an agent legitimately sees hidden cards. That knowledge then informs whether to hold up counter mana: an agent that has revealed the opponent's hand and seen no castable threat stops wasting two lands guarding a Counterspell and taps out for development instead. Without a reveal the agent knows nothing and behaves exactly as before.

author: reek
body: Can the opponent do anything at instant speed to punish an attack? Only if it holds cards AND has untapped mana to cast them. An empty hand or a tapped-out opponent cannot spring a combat trick or instant removal, so it is safe to press. Hand size and open mana are public; the belief model sharpens it -- if the agent has revealed the hand and seen no castable threat, it presses even into open mana.

author: reek
body: Public-zone observation. At the end of every turn each agent updates its belief about the opponent by looking at the zones anyone can see: the opponent's graveyard, exile, and the permanents it controls. This is not cheating -- those zones are open information -- but folding them into Knowledge gives the decision engine one place to ask "where is card X?" and, crucially, moves a card the agent had seen in hand (via a reveal) to its new home once it is cast, discarded, or exiled. So an agent keeps running state of what the opponent has cast, what has died or been discarded to the graveyard, and what has been exiled.

author: reek
body: Main-phase activated abilities. After casting, the AI activates its creatures' tap and sacrifice abilities. A tap ability (Tim-style ping, tap-to-draw, tap-to-gain) taps an untapped, non-summoning-sick creature and resolves the effect: damage pings the opponent's biggest creature, draw and gain go to the controller. A sacrifice ability fires only when it clearly trades up -- the sac damage would kill the opponent's biggest creature -- so the AI never throws a body away for nothing; sacrificing routes through destroy-permanent, so the sacrificed creature's own dies triggers still fire.

author: reek
body: Icy Manipulator: a "{cost}, {T}: Tap target permanent" activation. The AI fires it in the main phase against the opponent's biggest untapped creature -- tapping down a blocker before an attack, or a would-be attacker before their turn. Only fired when the opponent actually has an untapped creature to tap.

author: reek
body: A sacrifice-cost mana source (Black Lotus) is deliberately excluded from the greedy source-tapping: cracking it produces mana but destroys the card, so it must be spent on a real play, not dumped every main phase. is-tappable-source uses has-free-mana-ability, which ignores a FlexManaAbility whose cost is a sacrifice; maybe-crack-mana (below) is what cracks Lotus, and only to bridge a spell it can actually cast this turn.

author: reek
body: A pilot holding a counterspell leaves two lands untapped rather than tapping out, so it can answer a spell on the opponent's turn. tap-n-lands taps the first n untapped lands of a player; the rest stay up as interaction mana. Non-counter decks hold nothing and tap out as before.

author: reek
body: A responding player can pay with mana still in the pool plus whatever its untapped lands would make; when it casts, cast-instant taps those lands to produce the mana. This is why a pilot held two lands up.

author: reek
body: Black Lotus and its kin: a sacrifice-cost mana source is cracked only to enable a spell it bridges. maybe-crack-mana looks for an untapped sacrifice source the player controls and, if a non-land card in hand costs more than the current floating mana but no more than that plus what the source would add, taps it (which, being a sacrifice source, destroys it and adds its mana). The colour is chosen by the engine to match the hand's need, so a turn-one Lotus powers out the fatty it was held for and is never spent for nothing.

author: reek
body: A board sweeper (Wrath of God) is scored on the board differential, not as point removal: casting it is worth removal-priority per net creature it clears (opponent's creatures minus the caster's own, which also die). When the caster is not behind on creatures a sweep is bad, so it scores below the -1 floor and the pilot holds it -- control wraths only when it is losing the board.

author: reek
body: Armageddon (mass land destruction) is symmetric, so it is only good when the caster is ahead on the board: blow up everyone's lands while you have the creatures and the opponent cannot rebuild to answer them. Scored on the creature lead (aggression-weighted); below the -1 floor when not ahead, so the pilot holds it otherwise.

author: reek
body: Tranquility (destroy all enchantments) is symmetric, so it fires only when the opponent controls more enchantments than the caster -- otherwise it would blow up the caster's own anthem/aura, so it is held below the -1000 floor.

author: reek
body: Disenchant and Stone Rain destroy a targeted noncreature permanent (apply reuses apply-destroy). The AI targets the opponent's board: an artifact or enchantment for DestroyArtifact, a land for DestroyLand. First match is taken -- good enough for a pool where the opponent rarely has several.

author: reek
body: Regrowth targets the caster's own graveyard: the AI recurs its best card, the highest-mana-value one in the yard (a bomb or removal spell worth buying back). An empty graveyard yields no target and the spell is a harmless whiff.

author: reek
body: A creature the opponent cannot block gets its damage through, so it always attacks -- this is how a control deck actually closes: it flies its win-condition over a ground board turn after turn instead of durdling to the turn limit. "Cannot block" means the opponent controls creatures but none of them can legally block this attacker (a flier over a ground board), not merely an empty board -- swinging into an empty board is a separate aggression call. The attack is not strictly free: declaring it hands the opponent an instant-speed window and information, so the cost is the gamble that they hold a response the attack enables -- a cost that falls to zero only when the opponent is tapped out. A vigilant attacker (Serra Angel) carries the smallest downside: it deals the damage AND stays untapped to block, so it never sacrifices defence to attack. The bet that flying the clock in beats sitting back is the right one for a win-condition, so the AI takes it. Every other creature keeps the existing gate: when the deck is committing to combat, non-dominated creatures swing and dominated ones swing only when it is free or the pilot is aggressive; when the deck is not committing, only the unblockable threats go.
